Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 86, verse 1–17 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1608) Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The verse ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ was revealed in Makkah." Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his History, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khalid al-ʿAdwani that he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the market of Thaqif, standing on a bow or a staff, when he came to them seeking their support. He heard him reciting ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ until he finished it. He said: "I memorized it in the Jahiliyyah, then I recited it in Islam." He said: "Thaqif summoned me and said: 'What did you hear from this man?' So I recited it to them. Those of Quraysh who were with them said: 'We know our companion better. If we knew that what he says is true, we would have followed him.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾. Allah, glorified is He, swore by the sky and the night-visitant, and the night-visitant is the piercing star, as the revelation explicitly states.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: Allah swore by the sky and the night-visitant, meaning the stars, which visit at night and hide by day.

al-Farra' said: The night-visitant is the star, because it rises at night, and whatever comes to you at night is a ṭāriq (visitor).

Likewise said al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And like you, a pregnant woman has visited, and a nursing one; I distracted her from the one with amulets, the weaned child.*

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*We are the daughters of the night-visitor, walking upon the cushions.*

That is, our fathers in nobility are like the shining star. The root of ṭurūq is knocking, so the one who travels at night is called a ṭāriq because he needs to knock to arrive.

Some said that ṭurūq may occur by day, and the Arabs say: "I came to you today ṭarqatayn," meaning twice. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from the evil of the night's and day's visitors, except a visitor who visits with good."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what the ṭāriq is, magnifying its status after glorifying it by swearing by it, and He said: ﴿And what will make you know what the night-visitant is? The piercing star.﴾ The piercing (thāqib) is the shining one. From it is said: "the star pierced (thaqaba), piercing and brilliance (thaqāba), when it shone," and its thuqub is its light. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He spread it among the people until it was as if on a height a fire had been kindled with its thuqub.*

Al-Wahidi said: The term ṭāriq applies to anything that visits at night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have known what was meant by it had he not explained it by saying: ﴿the piercing star﴾. Mujahid said: al-thāqib is al-mutawahhij (the blazing one).

Sufyan said: Everything in the Qur'an with "wa-ma adraka" (and what will make you know), He informed him of it; and everything in which He said "wa-ma yudrika" (and what will make you know), He did not inform him of it.

The nominative of ﴿the piercing star﴾ is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a new one answering an implied question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" and it was answered: "It is the piercing star."

﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical. The readers' disagreement over lamma was mentioned in Surah Hud. Whoever reads it with the light pronunciation, then in (inna) here is the light form of the heavy (inna), with an implied pronoun of the matter as its subject, and the lam is the distinguishing lam. And ma is extra: that is, indeed the matter is that every soul, over it is a guardian. Whoever reads it with the heavy pronunciation, then in (in) is negating, and lamma means "except": that is, not every soul except that over it is a guardian. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read it here with the heavy pronunciation.

The rest read it with the light pronunciation.

It was said that the guardians (ḥāfiẓ) are the guardian angels who keep record of their deeds, words and actions, and count whatever good and evil they earn. It was said: the guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: it is reason, which guides them to what is beneficial and restrains them from what is harmful.

The first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], and His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [al-Anʿam: 61], and His saying: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. The true Guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 64], and the angels' guarding is from His guarding, since they act by His command.

﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾. The fa' indicates that the fact that over every soul there is a guardian obliges man to reflect on the beginning of his creation, so that he may know the power of Allah over what is less than that, namely resurrection.

Muqatil said: It means the one who denies resurrection: "from what he was created" — from what thing Allah created him. The meaning is: let him look with the look of reflection and inference until he knows that the One who began him from a drop of semen is able to restore him.

﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾. The sentence is a new one answering an implied question. The water is the seminal fluid (maniy), and the daf' is pouring. It is said: "I poured the water," meaning I poured it. It is said: "a gushing water" meaning one that is poured, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qariʿah: 7], meaning pleasing.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: "gushing water" means water poured into the womb.

al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz often use the active participle with the meaning of the passive in much of their speech, such as "a hidden secret" meaning a concealed one, "hunting" (?) meaning hunted, and "a sleeping night" and similar.

al-Zajjaj said: "from gushing water," that is, water with ejaculation. It is said: dāriʿ, qāyis and nābil, meaning possessor of armour, bow and arrow. Allah, glorified is He, meant the water of the man and the woman, since the human being is created from both; but He made them one water because they are mixed.

Then He described this water, saying: ﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs﴾, that is, from the loins of the man and the ribs of the woman (p-1609). The tarā'ib are the plural of tarība, which is the place of the necklace on the chest, and a child is only from the two waters.

The majority read yakhruju (it emerges) in the active voice. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn Miqsam read it in the passive voice.

As for ṣulb (loins), which is the back, there are several dialect forms. The majority read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and sukūn on the lām; the people of Makkah read it with a ḍammah on both the ṣād and the lām; al-Yamani read it with a fatḥah on both. It is said ṣālib on the pattern of qālib.

From it is the saying of al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib:

*You were transferred from loins to wombs*

in his famous verses in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ).

A discussion of this was given earlier when explaining His saying: ﴿those from your loins﴾ [al-Nisa': 23]. It was also said that the tarā'ib are what lies between the two breasts.

al-Dahhak said: the tarā'ib of the woman are the two hands, the two feet and the two eyes.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the neck.

Mujahid said: they are what lies between the shoulders and the chest.

It is also narrated from him that he said: they are the chest, and it is also narrated from him that he said: they are the collarbones.

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are the essence of the heart, from which the child is produced; but the well-known meaning in the language is that they are the bones of the chest and the upper breastbone. From it is the saying of Duraid ibn al-Simmah:

*If you turn your backs, we shall seize you on your backs; and if you come forward, we shall seize you on your tarā'ib.*

ʿIkrimah said: the tarā'ib are the chest, and he recited:

*A string of pearls upon her tarā'ib*

In al-Sihah: al-tarība is the singular of tarā'ib, and they are the bones of the chest. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the plural of tarība is tarīb. From it is the saying of al-Muthaqqab al-ʿAbdi:

*And of gold set upon a tarīb, like the colour of ivory, without wrinkles*

and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Her tarā'ib are polished like a mirror*

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest.

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the tarā'ib of the woman.

al-Farra' related that such a usage is found among the Arabs, where min bayn means min (from), and it was said that the man's water descends from the brain, and this does not contradict what is in the verse, because when it descends from the brain it descends from between the loins and the ribs. It was also said that the meaning is: it emerges from all parts of the body, and this does not contradict the verse, because the attribution of its emergence to between the loins and the ribs is based on the fact that most parts of the body are the loins and the ribs and what is adjacent to them and above them, from which it descends.

﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾. The pronoun in innahu refers to Allah, glorified is He, by the indication of the word "created" (khuliqa), since the One who created him is Allah, glorified is He. The pronoun in rajʿihi refers to man, and the meaning is: indeed Allah, glorified is He, is able, upon creating man, that is, to restore him by resurrection after death. Thus said a group of exegetes. Mujahid said: "to return the water into the urethra." ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak said: "to return the water into the loins." Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "If I wish, I will return him from old age to youth, from youth to childhood, from childhood to a drop." Ibn Zayd said: "He is able to hold back that water so that it does not emerge." The first is more apparent, and it was preferred by Ibn Jarir, al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi.

﴿On the day the secrets are tested﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase, according to the first interpretation, is "return him", and it was said that it is "able". It was objected that this implies restricting power to this day. It was said that the governing element is an implied one: that is, He returns him on the day the secrets are tested. It was also said that the governing element is an implied one, namely "remember", so that it is a direct object. As for those who say the meaning is the return of the water, the governing element of the adverbial phrase is an implied "remember". The meaning of "tubla as-sara'ir" is: they are tested and made known. From it is the saying of the rajiz:

*You used to belittle me before today; today I will test you, and you will test me*

That is: I will test you and you will test me, and I will examine you and you will examine me. The "secrets" are what is kept hidden in hearts of beliefs, intentions and other things; and what is meant here is the presentation of deeds and the publishing of records, so that at that time the good is distinguished from the evil, and the lean from the fat.

﴿Then he will have no power nor any helper﴾. That is: then man will have no power in himself by which he can defend himself against the punishment of Allah, nor any helper who can help him against what has befallen him.

ʿIkrimah said: these kings, on the Day of Resurrection, will have no power nor helper. Sufyan said: "power" is the clan, and "helper" is the ally; the first is preferable.

﴿By the sky of return﴾. Al-raj' is the rain.

al-Zajjaj said: al-raj' is rain, because it comes, returns and recurs.

al-Khalil said: al-raj' is the rain itself, and al-raj' is the spring vegetation.

The lexicographers said: al-raj' is rain.

al-Mutanakhkhil, describing a sword of his, said:

*White like the raj', deeply penetrating, when it spreads in an assembly, it cuts.*

al-Wahidi said: al-raj' is rain according to the statement of all the exegetes; but there is something to consider in this which he attributed to all the exegetes, for Ibn Zayd said: al-raj' is the sun, the moon and the stars, which return in the sky, rising from one side and setting on another.

Some exegetes said: dhat al-raj' means the possessor of the angels, because they return to it with the deeds of the servants.

Some said: the meaning of dhat al-raj' is dhat al-naf' (possessor of benefit). The reason the rain is called raj' is what al-Qaffal said: it is derived from tarjī' al-sawt (repetition of a sound), which is repeating it; likewise the rain, because it returns time after time, it was called raj'.

It was also said that the Arabs used to claim that the cloud carries water from the seas of the earth, then returns it to the earth. It was said the Arabs named it raj' for the sake of optimism, that it might return to them. It was said that it is because Allah returns it time after time.

﴿By the earth of the cleft﴾. It is what the earth splits open to bring forth plants, fruits and trees. al-Sad' is a split, because it cleaves the earth, so the earth cleaves for it.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it splits open with vegetation.

Mujahid said: "and the earth of pathways," which the waters split; it was said: "possessor of tillage," because it splits it; it was said: "possessor of the dead," because they split open from them at the resurrection.

The summary is that if al-sad' is the name of vegetation, the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing vegetation"; and if it means a cleft, then the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing the cleft from which vegetation and the like emerge."

The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that is: indeed the Qur'an is a word that distinguishes (p-1610) between truth and falsehood by making clear each of the two.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 86, verses 1–17 (part 2 of 2):

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:
"It makes us serious every day, and it jests."
﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.
﴿So give respite to the disbelievers.﴾ That is, delay them, and do not ask Allah, glorified is He, to hasten their destruction; be content with what He arranges for you in their affairs. His saying ﴿give them respite﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "give respite" (mahhil).
Mahhil and amhil have the same meaning, like nazzil and anzil. Al-imhal means al-intizar (granting delay), and tamahhala fi al-amr means he took his time over the matter (ittada'a). The accusative of ruwaydan is either as an emphatic infinitive verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for the mentioned verb, or as an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun: that is, "give them respite, a gentle respite," i.e., near or little.
Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." It occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in sara al-qawmu ruwaydan, meaning "they went along taking their time." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿By the heaven and the Tariq﴾, that he said: Your Lord swore by the Tariq. Everything that visits you at night is a tariq.
Ibn Jarir narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾, that he said: Over every soul are guardians from among the angels.
'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿The piercing star﴾, that he said: The shining star. ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾: he said: Except that over it is a guardian.
'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him ﴿He comes forth from between the loins and the ribs﴾, that he said: what is between the neck and the chest.
Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: The tariba of the woman, which is the place of the necklace.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him as well, that he said: The taraʼib are between the breasts of the woman.
al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well, that he said: The taraʼib are the four ribs on each side from the lower part of the ribs.
'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him as well ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾, that he said: Able to make the old man young and the young man old.
'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh, through several chains, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿By the heaven of the return﴾, that he said: rain after rain. ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾, he said: its splitting for vegetation.
Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾: the splitting of the valleys.
Ibn Manda and al-Daylami narrated from Mu'adh ibn Anas, traced to the Prophet, ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾, he said: it splits by the permission of Allah for wealth and vegetation.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that he said: true. ﴿And it is not a jest﴾, he said: not falsehood. And regarding His saying ﴿Give them respite, gently﴾, he said: a little.

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the tarā'ib of the woman.

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:
"It makes us serious every day, and it jests."
﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.
﴿So give respite to the disbelievers.﴾ That is, delay them, and do not ask Allah, glorified is He, to hasten their destruction; be content with what He arranges for you in their affairs. His saying ﴿give them respite﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "give respite" (mahhil).
Mahhil and amhil have the same meaning, like nazzil and anzil. Al-imhal means al-intizar (granting delay), and tamahhala fi al-amr means he took his time over the matter (ittada'a). Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." It occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in sara al-qawmu ruwaydan, meaning "they went along taking their time." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.

Commentary of al-Shawkani (Fath al-Qadir) on surah 86, verse 1–17 (part 1 of 2):

(p-1608) Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The verse ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ was revealed in Makkah." Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his History, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khalid al-ʿAdwani that he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the market of Thaqif, standing on a bow or a staff, when he came to them seeking their support. He heard him reciting ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ until he finished it. He said: "I memorized it in the Jahiliyyah, then I recited it in Islam." He said: "Thaqif summoned me and said: 'What did you hear from this man?' So I recited it to them. Those of Quraysh who were with them said: 'We know our companion better. If we knew that what he says is true, we would have followed him.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾. Allah, glorified is He, swore by the sky and the night-visitant, and the night-visitant is the piercing star, as the revelation explicitly states.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: Allah swore by the sky and the night-visitant, meaning the stars, which visit at night and hide by day.

al-Farra' said: The night-visitant is the star, because it rises at night, and whatever comes to you at night is a ṭāriq (visitor).

Likewise said al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And like you, a pregnant woman has visited, and a nursing one; I distracted her from the one with amulets, the weaned child.*

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*We are the daughters of the night-visitor, walking upon the cushions.*

That is, our fathers in nobility are like the shining star. The root of ṭurūq is knocking, so the one who travels at night is called a ṭāriq because he needs to knock to arrive.

Some said that ṭurūq may occur by day, and the Arabs say: "I came to you today ṭarqatayn," meaning twice. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from the evil of the night's and day's visitors, except a visitor who visits with good."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what the ṭāriq is, magnifying its status after glorifying it by swearing by it, and He said: ﴿And what will make you know what the night-visitant is? The piercing star.﴾ The piercing (thāqib) is the shining one. From it is said: "the star pierced (thaqaba), piercing and brilliance (thaqāba), when it shone," and its thuqub is its light. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He spread it among the people until it was as if on a height a fire had been kindled with its thuqub.*

Al-Wahidi said: The term ṭāriq applies to anything that visits at night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have known what was meant by it had he not explained it by saying: ﴿the piercing star﴾. Mujahid said: al-thāqib is al-mutawahhij (the blazing one).

Sufyan said: Everything in the Qur'an with "wa-ma adraka" (and what will make you know), He informed him of it; and everything in which He said "wa-ma yudrika" (and what will make you know), He did not inform him of it.

The nominative of ﴿the piercing star﴾ is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a new one answering an implied question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" and it was answered: "It is the piercing star."

Whoever reads it with the light pronunciation, then in (inna) here is the light form of the heavy (inna), with an implied pronoun of the matter as its subject, and the lam is the distinguishing lam. And ma is extra: that is, indeed the matter is that every soul, over it is a guardian. Whoever reads it with the heavy pronunciation, then in (in) is negating, and lamma means "except": that is, not every soul except that over it is a guardian. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read it here with the heavy pronunciation.

The rest read it with the light pronunciation.

It was said that the guardians (ḥāfiẓ) are the guardian angels who keep record of their deeds, words and actions, and count whatever good and evil they earn. It was said: the guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: it is reason, which guides them to what is beneficial and restrains them from what is harmful.

The first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], and His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [al-Anʿam: 61], and His saying: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. The true Guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 64], and the angels' guarding is from His guarding, since they act by His command.

﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾. The fa' indicates that the fact that over every soul there is a guardian obliges man to reflect on the beginning of his creation, so that he may know the power of Allah over what is less than that, namely resurrection.

Muqatil said: It means the one who denies resurrection: "from what he was created" — from what thing Allah created him. The meaning is: let him look with the look of reflection and inference until he knows that the One who began him from a drop of semen is able to restore him.

﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾. The sentence is a new one answering an implied question. The water is the seminal fluid (maniy), and the daf' is pouring. It is said: "I poured the water," meaning I poured it. It is said: "a gushing water" meaning one that is poured, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qariʿah: 7], meaning pleasing.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: "gushing water" means water poured into the womb.

al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz often use the active participle with the meaning of the passive in much of their speech, such as "a hidden secret" meaning a concealed one, "hunting" (?) meaning hunted, and "a sleeping night" and similar.

al-Zajjaj said: "from gushing water," that is, water with ejaculation. It is said: dāriʿ, qāyis and nābil, meaning possessor of armour, bow and arrow. Allah, glorified is He, meant the water of the man and the woman, since the human being is created from both; but He made them one water because they are mixed.

Then He described this water, saying: ﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs﴾, that is, from the loins of the man and the ribs of the woman (p-1609). The tarā'ib are the plural of tarība, which is the place of the necklace on the chest, and a child is only from the two waters.

The majority read yakhruju (it emerges) in the active voice. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn Miqsam read it in the passive voice.

As for ṣulb (loins), which is the back, there are several dialect forms. The majority read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and sukūn on the lām; the people of Makkah read it with a ḍammah on both the ṣād and the lām; al-Yamani read it with a fatḥah on both. It is said ṣālib on the pattern of qālib.

*You were transferred from loins to wombs*

in his famous verses in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ).

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the neck.

Mujahid said: they are what lies between the shoulders and the chest.

It is also narrated from him that he said: they are the chest, and it is also narrated from him that he said: they are the collarbones.

*If you turn your backs, we shall seize you on your backs; and if you come forward, we shall seize you on your tarā'ib.*

ʿIkrimah said: the tarā'ib are the chest, and he recited:

*A string of pearls upon her tarā'ib*

*And of gold set upon a tarīb, like the colour of ivory, without wrinkles*

and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Her tarā'ib are polished like a mirror*

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest.

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the tarā'ib of the woman.

It was also said that the meaning is: it emerges from all parts of the body, and this does not contradict the verse, because the attribution of its emergence to between the loins and the ribs is based on the fact that most parts of the body are the loins and the ribs and what is adjacent to them and above them, from which it descends.

﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾. The pronoun in innahu refers to Allah, glorified is He, by the indication of the word "created" (khuliqa), since the One who created him is Allah, glorified is He. Thus said a group of exegetes. Mujahid said: "to return the water into the urethra." ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak said: "to return the water into the loins." Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "If I wish, I will return him from old age to youth, from youth to childhood, from childhood to a drop." Ibn Zayd said: "He is able to hold back that water so that it does not emerge." The first is more apparent, and it was preferred by Ibn Jarir, al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi.

﴿On the day the secrets are tested﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase, according to the first interpretation, is "return him", and it was said that it is "able". It was objected that this implies restricting power to this day. It was said that the governing element is an implied one: that is, He returns him on the day the secrets are tested. It was also said that the governing element is an implied one, namely "remember", so that it is a direct object. As for those who say the meaning is the return of the water, the governing element of the adverbial phrase is an implied "remember". The meaning of "tubla as-sara'ir" is: they are tested and made known. From it is the saying of the rajiz:

*You used to belittle me before today; today I will test you, and you will test me*

That is: I will test you and you will test me, and I will examine you and you will examine me. The "secrets" are what is kept hidden in hearts of beliefs, intentions and other things; and what is meant here is the presentation of deeds and the publishing of records, so that at that time the good is distinguished from the evil, and the lean from the fat.

﴿Then he will have no power nor any helper﴾. That is: then man will have no power in himself by which he can defend himself against the punishment of Allah, nor any helper who can help him against what has befallen him.

ʿIkrimah said: these kings, on the Day of Resurrection, will have no power nor helper. Sufyan said: "power" is the clan, and "helper" is the ally; the first is preferable.

﴿By the sky of return﴾. Al-raj' is the rain.

al-Zajjaj said: al-raj' is rain, because it comes, returns and recurs.

al-Khalil said: al-raj' is the rain itself, and al-raj' is the spring vegetation.

The lexicographers said: al-raj' is rain.

al-Mutanakhkhil, describing a sword of his, said:

*White like the raj', deeply penetrating, when it spreads in an assembly, it cuts.*

al-Wahidi said: al-raj' is rain according to the statement of all the exegetes; but there is something to consider in this which he attributed to all the exegetes, for Ibn Zayd said: al-raj' is the sun, the moon and the stars, which return in the sky, rising from one side and setting on another.

Some exegetes said: dhat al-raj' means the possessor of the angels, because they return to it with the deeds of the servants.

Some said: the meaning of dhat al-raj' is dhat al-naf' (possessor of benefit). The reason the rain is called raj' is what al-Qaffal said: it is derived from tarjī' al-sawt (repetition of a sound), which is repeating it; likewise the rain, because it returns time after time, it was called raj'.

It was also said that the Arabs used to claim that the cloud carries water from the seas of the earth, then returns it to the earth. It was said the Arabs named it raj' for the sake of optimism, that it might return to them. It was said that it is because Allah returns it time after time.

﴿By the earth of the cleft﴾. It is what the earth splits open to bring forth plants, fruits and trees. al-Sad' is a split, because it cleaves the earth, so the earth cleaves for it.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it splits open with vegetation.

Mujahid said: "and the earth of pathways," which the waters split; it was said: "possessor of tillage," because it splits it; it was said: "possessor of the dead," because they split open from them at the resurrection.

The summary is that if al-sad' is the name of vegetation, the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing vegetation"; and if it means a cleft, then the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing the cleft from which vegetation and the like emerge."

The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that is: indeed the Qur'an is a word that distinguishes (p-1610) between truth and falsehood by making clear each of the two.

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:
"It makes us serious every day, and it jests."
﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.
﴿So give respite to the disbelievers.﴾ That is, delay them, and do not ask Allah, glorified is He, to hasten their destruction; be content with what He arranges for you in their affairs. His saying ﴿give them respite﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "give respite" (mahhil).
Mahhil and amhil have the same meaning, like nazzil and anzil. Al-imhal means al-intizar (granting delay), and tamahhala fi al-amr means he took his time over the matter (ittada'a). The accusative of ruwaydan is either as an emphatic infinitive verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for the mentioned verb, or as an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun: that is, "give them respite, a gentle respite," i.e., near or little.
Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." It occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in sara al-qawmu ruwaydan, meaning "they went along taking their time." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿By the heaven and the Tariq﴾, that he said: Your Lord swore by the Tariq. Everything that visits you at night is a tariq.
Ibn Jarir narrated from him, regarding His saying ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾, that he said: Over every soul are guardians from among the angels.
'Abd ibn Humayd, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, and Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿The piercing star﴾, that he said: The shining star. ﴿There is no soul but that over it is a guardian﴾: he said: Except that over it is a guardian.
'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him ﴿He comes forth from between the loins and the ribs﴾, that he said: what is between the neck and the chest.
Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: The tariba of the woman, which is the place of the necklace.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him as well, that he said: The taraʼib are between the breasts of the woman.
al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well, that he said: The taraʼib are the four ribs on each side from the lower part of the ribs.
'Abd ibn Humayd and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him as well ﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾, that he said: Able to make the old man young and the young man old.
'Abd al-Razzaq, al-Firyabi, 'Abd ibn Humayd, al-Bukhari in his History, Ibn Jarir, Ibn al-Mundhir, Ibn Abi Hatim, Abu al-Shaykh in al-'Azama, and al-Hakim, who authenticated it, and Ibn Mardawayh, through several chains, narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿By the heaven of the return﴾, that he said: rain after rain. ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾, he said: its splitting for vegetation.
Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾: the splitting of the valleys.
Ibn Manda and al-Daylami narrated from Mu'adh ibn Anas, traced to the Prophet, ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾, he said: it splits by the permission of Allah for wealth and vegetation.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that he said: true. ﴿And it is not a jest﴾, he said: not falsehood. And regarding His saying ﴿Give them respite, gently﴾, he said: a little.

Some said: the meaning of dhat al-raj' is dhat al-naf' (possessor of benefit). The reason the rain is called raj' is what al-Qaffal said: it is derived from tarjī' al-sawt (repetition of a sound), which is repeating it; likewise the rain, because it returns time after time, it was called raj'.

﴿By the earth of the cleft﴾. It is what the earth splits open to bring forth plants, fruits and trees. al-Sad' is a split, because it cleaves the earth, so the earth cleaves for it.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it splits open with vegetation.

Mujahid said: "and the earth of pathways," which the waters split; it was said: "possessor of tillage," because it splits it; it was said: "possessor of the dead," because they split open from them at the resurrection.

The summary is that if al-sad' is the name of vegetation, the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing vegetation"; and if it means a cleft, then the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing the cleft from which vegetation and the like emerge."

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:

﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.

He heard him reciting ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ until he finished it. He said: "I memorized it in the Jahiliyyah, then I recited it in Islam." He said: "Thaqif summoned me and said: 'What did you hear from this man?' So I recited it to them. Those of Quraysh who were with them said: 'We know our companion better. In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾. Allah, glorified is He, swore by the sky and the night-visitant, and the night-visitant is the piercing star, as the revelation explicitly states.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: Allah swore by the sky and the night-visitant, meaning the stars, which visit at night and hide by day.

al-Farra' said: The night-visitant is the star, because it rises at night, and whatever comes to you at night is a ṭāriq (visitor).

Likewise said al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And like you, a pregnant woman has visited, and a nursing one; I distracted her from the one with amulets, the weaned child.*

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*We are the daughters of the night-visitor, walking upon the cushions.*

That is, our fathers in nobility are like the shining star. The root of ṭurūq is knocking, so the one who travels at night is called a ṭāriq because he needs to knock to arrive.

Some said that ṭurūq may occur by day, and the Arabs say: "I came to you today ṭarqatayn," meaning twice. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from the evil of the night's and day's visitors, except a visitor who visits with good."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what the ṭāriq is, magnifying its status after glorifying it by swearing by it, and He said: ﴿And what will make you know what the night-visitant is? The piercing star.﴾ The piercing (thāqib) is the shining one. From it is said: "the star pierced (thaqaba), piercing and brilliance (thaqāba), when it shone," and its thuqub is its light. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He spread it among the people until it was as if on a height a fire had been kindled with its thuqub.*

Al-Wahidi said: The term ṭāriq applies to anything that visits at night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have known what was meant by it had he not explained it by saying: ﴿the piercing star﴾. Mujahid said: al-thāqib is al-mutawahhij (the blazing one).

Sufyan said: Everything in the Qur'an with "wa-ma adraka" (and what will make you know), He informed him of it; and everything in which He said "wa-ma yudrika" (and what will make you know), He did not inform him of it.

The nominative of ﴿the piercing star﴾ is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a new one answering an implied question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" and it was answered: "It is the piercing star."

﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical. The readers' disagreement over lamma was mentioned in Surah Hud. Whoever reads it with the light pronunciation, then in (inna) here is the light form of the heavy (inna), with an implied pronoun of the matter as its subject, and the lam is the distinguishing lam. And ma is extra: that is, indeed the matter is that every soul, over it is a guardian. Whoever reads it with the heavy pronunciation, then in (in) is negating, and lamma means "except": that is, not every soul except that over it is a guardian. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read it here with the heavy pronunciation.

The rest read it with the light pronunciation.

It was said that the guardians (ḥāfiẓ) are the guardian angels who keep record of their deeds, words and actions, and count whatever good and evil they earn. It was said: the guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: it is reason, which guides them to what is beneficial and restrains them from what is harmful.

The first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], and His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [al-Anʿam: 61], and His saying: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. The true Guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 64], and the angels' guarding is from His guarding, since they act by His command.

﴿So let man look at what he was created from﴾. The fa' indicates that the fact that over every soul there is a guardian obliges man to reflect on the beginning of his creation, so that he may know the power of Allah over what is less than that, namely resurrection.

Muqatil said: It means the one who denies resurrection: "from what he was created" — from what thing Allah created him. The meaning is: let him look with the look of reflection and inference until he knows that the One who began him from a drop of semen is able to restore him.

﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾. The sentence is a new one answering an implied question. The water is the seminal fluid (maniy), and the daf' is pouring. It is said: "I poured the water," meaning I poured it. It is said: "a gushing water" meaning one that is poured, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qariʿah: 7], meaning pleasing.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: "gushing water" means water poured into the womb.

al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz often use the active participle with the meaning of the passive in much of their speech, such as "a hidden secret" meaning a concealed one, "hunting" (?) meaning hunted, and "a sleeping night" and similar.

al-Zajjaj said: "from gushing water," that is, water with ejaculation. It is said: dāriʿ, qāyis and nābil, meaning possessor of armour, bow and arrow. Allah, glorified is He, meant the water of the man and the woman, since the human being is created from both; but He made them one water because they are mixed.

Then He described this water, saying: ﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs﴾, that is, from the loins of the man and the ribs of the woman (p-1609). The tarā'ib are the plural of tarība, which is the place of the necklace on the chest, and a child is only from the two waters.

The majority read yakhruju (it emerges) in the active voice. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn Miqsam read it in the passive voice.

*You were transferred from loins to wombs*

in his famous verses in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Dahhak said: the tarā'ib of the woman are the two hands, the two feet and the two eyes.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the neck.

Mujahid said: they are what lies between the shoulders and the chest.

It is also narrated from him that he said: they are the chest, and it is also narrated from him that he said: they are the collarbones.

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are the essence of the heart, from which the child is produced; but the well-known meaning in the language is that they are the bones of the chest and the upper breastbone. From it is the saying of Duraid ibn al-Simmah:

*If you turn your backs, we shall seize you on your backs; and if you come forward, we shall seize you on your tarā'ib.*

ʿIkrimah said: the tarā'ib are the chest, and he recited:

*A string of pearls upon her tarā'ib*

*And of gold set upon a tarīb, like the colour of ivory, without wrinkles*

*Her tarā'ib are polished like a mirror*

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the tarā'ib of the woman.

﴿Indeed, He is able to return him﴾. The pronoun in innahu refers to Allah, glorified is He, by the indication of the word "created" (khuliqa), since the One who created him is Allah, glorified is He. ﴿On the day the secrets are tested﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase, according to the first interpretation, is "return him", and it was said that it is "able". *You used to belittle me before today; today I will test you, and you will test me*

al-Zajjaj said: al-raj' is rain, because it comes, returns and recurs.

al-Khalil said: al-raj' is the rain itself, and al-raj' is the spring vegetation.

The lexicographers said: al-raj' is rain.

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*White like the raj', deeply penetrating, when it spreads in an assembly, it cuts.*

al-Wahidi said: al-raj' is rain according to the statement of all the exegetes; but there is something to consider in this which he attributed to all the exegetes, for Ibn Zayd said: al-raj' is the sun, the moon and the stars, which return in the sky, rising from one side and setting on another.

Some said: the meaning of dhat al-raj' is dhat al-naf' (possessor of benefit). The reason the rain is called raj' is what al-Qaffal said: it is derived from tarjī' al-sawt (repetition of a sound), which is repeating it; likewise the rain, because it returns time after time, it was called raj'.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it splits open with vegetation.

The summary is that if al-sad' is the name of vegetation, the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing vegetation"; and if it means a cleft, then the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing the cleft from which vegetation and the like emerge."

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:
"It makes us serious every day, and it jests."
﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.
﴿So give respite to the disbelievers.﴾ That is, delay them, and do not ask Allah, glorified is He, to hasten their destruction; be content with what He arranges for you in their affairs. His saying ﴿give them respite﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "give respite" (mahhil).
Mahhil and amhil have the same meaning, like nazzil and anzil. Al-imhal means al-intizar (granting delay), and tamahhala fi al-amr means he took his time over the matter (ittada'a). The accusative of ruwaydan is either as an emphatic infinitive verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for the mentioned verb, or as an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun: that is, "give them respite, a gentle respite," i.e., near or little.
Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." It occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in sara al-qawmu ruwaydan, meaning "they went along taking their time." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.
Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Ibn 'Abbas, regarding His saying ﴿By the heaven and the Tariq﴾, that he said: Your Lord swore by the Tariq. Everything that visits you at night is a tariq.

Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾: the splitting of the valleys.
Ibn Manda and al-Daylami narrated from Mu'adh ibn Anas, traced to the Prophet, ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾, he said: it splits by the permission of Allah for wealth and vegetation.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that he said: true. ﴿And it is not a jest﴾, he said: not falsehood. And regarding His saying ﴿Give them respite, gently﴾, he said: a little.

Thus said a group of exegetes. Mujahid said: "to return the water into the urethra." ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak said: "to return the water into the loins." That is: I will test you and you will test me, and I will examine you and you will examine me. The lexicographers said: al-raj' is rain.

Some said: the meaning of dhat al-raj' is dhat al-naf' (possessor of benefit). The reason the rain is called raj' is what al-Qaffal said: it is derived from tarjī' al-sawt (repetition of a sound), which is repeating it; likewise the rain, because it returns time after time, it was called raj'.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it splits open with vegetation.

Mujahid said: "and the earth of pathways," which the waters split; it was said: "possessor of tillage," because it splits it; it was said: "possessor of the dead," because they split open from them at the resurrection.

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:
"It makes us serious every day, and it jests."
﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.

Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.

Likewise said al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And like you, a pregnant woman has visited, and a nursing one; I distracted her from the one with amulets, the weaned child.*

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*We are the daughters of the night-visitor, walking upon the cushions.*

(p-1608) Ibn al-Durays, al-Nahhas, Ibn Mardawayh and al-Bayhaqi narrated from Ibn ʿAbbas, who said: "The verse ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ was revealed in Makkah." Ahmad, al-Bukhari in his History, al-Tabarani and Ibn Mardawayh narrated from Khalid al-ʿAdwani that he saw the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) in the market of Thaqif, standing on a bow or a staff, when he came to them seeking their support. He heard him reciting ﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾ until he finished it. He said: "I memorized it in the Jahiliyyah, then I recited it in Islam." He said: "Thaqif summoned me and said: 'What did you hear from this man?' So I recited it to them. Those of Quraysh who were with them said: 'We know our companion better. If we knew that what he says is true, we would have followed him.'"

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

﴿By the sky and the night-visitant﴾. Allah, glorified is He, swore by the sky and the night-visitant, and the night-visitant is the piercing star, as the revelation explicitly states.

Al-Wahidi said: The exegetes said: Allah swore by the sky and the night-visitant, meaning the stars, which visit at night and hide by day.

al-Farra' said: The night-visitant is the star, because it rises at night, and whatever comes to you at night is a ṭāriq (visitor).

Likewise said al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And like you, a pregnant woman has visited, and a nursing one; I distracted her from the one with amulets, the weaned child.*

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*We are the daughters of the night-visitor, walking upon the cushions.*

That is, our fathers in nobility are like the shining star. The root of ṭurūq is knocking, so the one who travels at night is called a ṭāriq because he needs to knock to arrive.

Some said that ṭurūq may occur by day, and the Arabs say: "I came to you today ṭarqatayn," meaning twice. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from the evil of the night's and day's visitors, except a visitor who visits with good."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what the ṭāriq is, magnifying its status after glorifying it by swearing by it, and He said: ﴿And what will make you know what the night-visitant is? The piercing star.﴾ The piercing (thāqib) is the shining one. From it is said: "the star pierced (thaqaba), piercing and brilliance (thaqāba), when it shone," and its thuqub is its light. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He spread it among the people until it was as if on a height a fire had been kindled with its thuqub.*

Al-Wahidi said: The term ṭāriq applies to anything that visits at night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have known what was meant by it had he not explained it by saying: ﴿the piercing star﴾. Mujahid said: al-thāqib is al-mutawahhij (the blazing one).

Sufyan said: Everything in the Qur'an with "wa-ma adraka" (and what will make you know), He informed him of it; and everything in which He said "wa-ma yudrika" (and what will make you know), He did not inform him of it.

The nominative of ﴿the piercing star﴾ is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a new one answering an implied question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" and it was answered: "It is the piercing star."

﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical. The readers' disagreement over lamma was mentioned in Surah Hud. Whoever reads it with the light pronunciation, then in (inna) here is the light form of the heavy (inna), with an implied pronoun of the matter as its subject, and the lam is the distinguishing lam. And ma is extra: that is, indeed the matter is that every soul, over it is a guardian. Whoever reads it with the heavy pronunciation, then in (in) is negating, and lamma means "except": that is, not every soul except that over it is a guardian. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read it here with the heavy pronunciation.

The rest read it with the light pronunciation.

It was said that the guardians (ḥāfiẓ) are the guardian angels who keep record of their deeds, words and actions, and count whatever good and evil they earn. It was said: the guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: it is reason, which guides them to what is beneficial and restrains them from what is harmful.

The first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], and His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [al-Anʿam: 61], and His saying: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. The true Guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 64], and the angels' guarding is from His guarding, since they act by His command.

Muqatil said: It means the one who denies resurrection: "from what he was created" — from what thing Allah created him. The meaning is: let him look with the look of reflection and inference until he knows that the One who began him from a drop of semen is able to restore him.

﴿He was created from a gushing fluid﴾. The sentence is a new one answering an implied question. The water is the seminal fluid (maniy), and the daf' is pouring. It is said: "I poured the water," meaning I poured it. It is said: "a gushing water" meaning one that is poured, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qariʿah: 7], meaning pleasing.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: "gushing water" means water poured into the womb.

al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz often use the active participle with the meaning of the passive in much of their speech, such as "a hidden secret" meaning a concealed one, "hunting" (?) meaning hunted, and "a sleeping night" and similar.

al-Zajjaj said: "from gushing water," that is, water with ejaculation. It is said: dāriʿ, qāyis and nābil, meaning possessor of armour, bow and arrow. Allah, glorified is He, meant the water of the man and the woman, since the human being is created from both; but He made them one water because they are mixed.

Then He described this water, saying: ﴿It emerges from between the loins and the ribs﴾, that is, from the loins of the man and the ribs of the woman (p-1609). The tarā'ib are the plural of tarība, which is the place of the necklace on the chest, and a child is only from the two waters.

The majority read yakhruju (it emerges) in the active voice. Ibn Abi ʿAbla and Ibn Miqsam read it in the passive voice.

As for ṣulb (loins), which is the back, there are several dialect forms. The majority read it with a ḍammah on the ṣād and sukūn on the lām; the people of Makkah read it with a ḍammah on both the ṣād and the lām; al-Yamani read it with a fatḥah on both. It is said ṣālib on the pattern of qālib.

From it is the saying of al-ʿAbbas ibn ʿAbd al-Muttalib:

*You were transferred from loins to wombs*

in his famous verses in praise of the Prophet (ﷺ).

al-Dahhak said: the tarā'ib of the woman are the two hands, the two feet and the two eyes.

Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the neck.

Mujahid said: they are what lies between the shoulders and the chest.

It is also narrated from him that he said: they are the chest, and it is also narrated from him that he said: they are the collarbones.

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are the essence of the heart, from which the child is produced; but the well-known meaning in the language is that they are the bones of the chest and the upper breastbone. From it is the saying of Duraid ibn al-Simmah:

*If you turn your backs, we shall seize you on your backs; and if you come forward, we shall seize you on your tarā'ib.*

ʿIkrimah said: the tarā'ib are the chest, and he recited:

*A string of pearls upon her tarā'ib*

In al-Sihah: al-tarība is the singular of tarā'ib, and they are the bones of the chest. Abu ʿUbaydah said: the plural of tarība is tarīb. From it is the saying of al-Muthaqqab al-ʿAbdi:

*And of gold set upon a tarīb, like the colour of ivory, without wrinkles*

and the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*Her tarā'ib are polished like a mirror*

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest.

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the tarā'ib of the woman.

al-Farra' related that such a usage is found among the Arabs, where min bayn means min (from), and it was said that the man's water descends from the brain, and this does not contradict what is in the verse, because when it descends from the brain it descends from between the loins and the ribs. It was also said that the meaning is: it emerges from all parts of the body, and this does not contradict the verse, because the attribution of its emergence to between the loins and the ribs is based on the fact that most parts of the body are the loins and the ribs and what is adjacent to them and above them, from which it descends.

Thus said a group of exegetes. Mujahid said: "to return the water into the urethra." ʿIkrimah and al-Dahhak said: "to return the water into the loins." Muqatil ibn Hayyan said: "If I wish, I will return him from old age to youth, from youth to childhood, from childhood to a drop." Ibn Zayd said: "He is able to hold back that water so that it does not emerge." The first is more apparent, and it was preferred by Ibn Jarir, al-Tha'labi and al-Qurtubi.

﴿On the day the secrets are tested﴾. The governing element of the adverbial phrase, according to the first interpretation, is "return him", and it was said that it is "able". It was objected that this implies restricting power to this day. It was said that the governing element is an implied one: that is, He returns him on the day the secrets are tested. It was also said that the governing element is an implied one, namely "remember", so that it is a direct object. As for those who say the meaning is the return of the water, the governing element of the adverbial phrase is an implied "remember". The meaning of "tubla as-sara'ir" is: they are tested and made known. From it is the saying of the rajiz:

*You used to belittle me before today; today I will test you, and you will test me*

That is: I will test you and you will test me, and I will examine you and you will examine me. The "secrets" are what is kept hidden in hearts of beliefs, intentions and other things; and what is meant here is the presentation of deeds and the publishing of records, so that at that time the good is distinguished from the evil, and the lean from the fat.

﴿Then he will have no power nor any helper﴾. That is: then man will have no power in himself by which he can defend himself against the punishment of Allah, nor any helper who can help him against what has befallen him.

ʿIkrimah said: these kings, on the Day of Resurrection, will have no power nor helper. Sufyan said: "power" is the clan, and "helper" is the ally; the first is preferable.

﴿By the sky of return﴾. Al-raj' is the rain.

al-Zajjaj said: al-raj' is rain, because it comes, returns and recurs.

al-Khalil said: al-raj' is the rain itself, and al-raj' is the spring vegetation.

The lexicographers said: al-raj' is rain.

al-Mutanakhkhil, describing a sword of his, said:

*White like the raj', deeply penetrating, when it spreads in an assembly, it cuts.*

al-Wahidi said: al-raj' is rain according to the statement of all the exegetes; but there is something to consider in this which he attributed to all the exegetes, for Ibn Zayd said: al-raj' is the sun, the moon and the stars, which return in the sky, rising from one side and setting on another.

Some exegetes said: dhat al-raj' means the possessor of the angels, because they return to it with the deeds of the servants.

Some said: the meaning of dhat al-raj' is dhat al-naf' (possessor of benefit). The reason the rain is called raj' is what al-Qaffal said: it is derived from tarjī' al-sawt (repetition of a sound), which is repeating it; likewise the rain, because it returns time after time, it was called raj'.

It was also said that the Arabs used to claim that the cloud carries water from the seas of the earth, then returns it to the earth. It was said the Arabs named it raj' for the sake of optimism, that it might return to them. It was said that it is because Allah returns it time after time.

﴿By the earth of the cleft﴾. It is what the earth splits open to bring forth plants, fruits and trees. al-Sad' is a split, because it cleaves the earth, so the earth cleaves for it.

Abu ʿUbaydah and al-Farra' said: it splits open with vegetation.

Mujahid said: "and the earth of pathways," which the waters split; it was said: "possessor of tillage," because it splits it; it was said: "possessor of the dead," because they split open from them at the resurrection.

The summary is that if al-sad' is the name of vegetation, the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing vegetation"; and if it means a cleft, then the meaning is as if He said: "by the earth possessing the cleft from which vegetation and the like emerge."

The answer to the oath is His saying: ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that is: indeed the Qur'an is a word that distinguishes (p-1610) between truth and falsehood by making clear each of the two.

Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.
﴿So give respite to the disbelievers.﴾ That is, delay them, and do not ask Allah, glorified is He, to hasten their destruction; be content with what He arranges for you in their affairs. His saying ﴿give them respite﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "give respite" (mahhil).
Mahhil and amhil have the same meaning, like nazzil and anzil. Al-imhal means al-intizar (granting delay), and tamahhala fi al-amr means he took his time over the matter (ittada'a). The accusative of ruwaydan is either as an emphatic infinitive verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for the mentioned verb, or as an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun: that is, "give them respite, a gentle respite," i.e., near or little.
Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." It occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in sara al-qawmu ruwaydan, meaning "they went along taking their time." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.

﴿And it is not a jest.﴾ That is, it was not sent down in play; rather, it is serious and not a jest. Al-hazl (jest) is the opposite of al-jidd (seriousness).
Al-Kumayt said:
"It makes us serious every day, and it jests."
﴿Indeed, they are plotting a plot.﴾ That is, they are scheming to nullify what the Messenger of Allah (ﷺ) brought of the true religion.
Al-Zajjaj said: They deceive the Prophet (ﷺ) and display what is contrary to what they hold.
﴿And I am plotting a plot.﴾ That is, I will draw them on gradually from where they do not know, and I will repay them for their plotting. It has been said that this refers to what Allah inflicted upon them on the Day of Badr of killing and capture.
﴿So give respite to the disbelievers.﴾ That is, delay them, and do not ask Allah, glorified is He, to hasten their destruction; be content with what He arranges for you in their affairs. His saying ﴿give them respite﴾ is a substitute (badal) for "give respite" (mahhil).
Mahhil and amhil have the same meaning, like nazzil and anzil. Al-imhal means al-intizar (granting delay), and tamahhala fi al-amr means he took his time over the matter (ittada'a). The accusative of ruwaydan is either as an emphatic infinitive verbal noun (maṣdar mu'akkid) for the mentioned verb, or as an adjective (na't) for an omitted verbal noun: that is, "give them respite, a gentle respite," i.e., near or little.
Abu 'Ubayda said: In the speech of the Arabs, ruwayd is a diminutive of rawd, and he recited:
"As if she walks upon a gentle pace."
That is, at a leisurely pace. It has also been said that it is a diminutive of arwad, a verbal noun of rawd, a diminutive of tarkhim. It also occurs as an imperative form (ism fi'l), as in ruwayda Zaydan, meaning "give him respite." It occurs as a circumstantial accusative (hal), as in sara al-qawmu ruwaydan, meaning "they went along taking their time." Al-Jawhari mentioned this meaning, and the full discussion belongs in the science of grammar.

Ibn Abi Hatim narrated from him regarding the verse, that he said: The tariba of the woman, which is the place of the necklace.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from him as well, that he said: The taraʼib are between the breasts of the woman.
al-Hakim narrated and authenticated from him as well, that he said: The taraʼib are the four ribs on each side from the lower part of the ribs.

Ibn Manda and al-Daylami narrated from Mu'adh ibn Anas, traced to the Prophet, ﴿And the earth of the splitting﴾, he said: it splits by the permission of Allah for wealth and vegetation.
Ibn Jarir and Ibn al-Mundhir narrated from Ibn 'Abbas regarding His saying ﴿Indeed, it is a decisive word﴾, that he said: true. ﴿And it is not a jest﴾, he said: not falsehood. And regarding His saying ﴿Give them respite, gently﴾, he said: a little.

In the name of Allah, the Most Gracious, the Most Merciful.

al-Farra' said: The night-visitant is the star, because it rises at night, and whatever comes to you at night is a ṭāriq (visitor).

Likewise said al-Zajjaj and al-Mubarrad. From it is the saying of Imru' al-Qays:

*And like you, a pregnant woman has visited, and a nursing one; I distracted her from the one with amulets, the weaned child.*

And his other saying:

*Did you not see me, whenever I came as a night-visitor, that I found in her a fragrance even though she had not perfumed herself?*

It has been disputed whether the ṭāriq is a specific star or the category of stars. It was said to be Saturn; it was said to be the Pleiades; it was said to be that by which the devils are pelted; and it was said to be the category of stars.

In al-Sihah (Al-Jawhari) said: The ṭāriq is the star called the Morning Star. From it is the saying of Hind bint ʿUtbah:

*We are the daughters of the night-visitor, walking upon the cushions.*

That is, our fathers in nobility are like the shining star. The root of ṭurūq is knocking, so the one who travels at night is called a ṭāriq because he needs to knock to arrive.

Some said that ṭurūq may occur by day, and the Arabs say: "I came to you today ṭarqatayn," meaning twice. From it is the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ): "I seek refuge in You from the evil of the night's and day's visitors, except a visitor who visits with good."

Then Allah, glorified is He, explained what the ṭāriq is, magnifying its status after glorifying it by swearing by it, and He said: ﴿And what will make you know what the night-visitant is? The piercing star.﴾ The piercing (thāqib) is the shining one. From it is said: "the star pierced (thaqaba), piercing and brilliance (thaqāba), when it shone," and its thuqub is its light. From it is the saying of the poet:

*He spread it among the people until it was as if on a height a fire had been kindled with its thuqub.*

Al-Wahidi said: The term ṭāriq applies to anything that visits at night, and the Prophet (ﷺ) would not have known what was meant by it had he not explained it by saying: ﴿the piercing star﴾. Mujahid said: al-thāqib is al-mutawahhij (the blazing one).

Sufyan said: Everything in the Qur'an with "wa-ma adraka" (and what will make you know), He informed him of it; and everything in which He said "wa-ma yudrika" (and what will make you know), He did not inform him of it.

The nominative of ﴿the piercing star﴾ is because it is the predicate of an omitted subject, and the sentence is a new one answering an implied question that arises from what precedes it, as if it were said: "What is it?" and it was answered: "It is the piercing star."

﴿Indeed, every soul has over it a guardian﴾. This is the answer to the oath, and what lies between them is a parenthetical. The readers' disagreement over lamma was mentioned in Surah Hud. Whoever reads it with the light pronunciation, then in (inna) here is the light form of the heavy (inna), with an implied pronoun of the matter as its subject, and the lam is the distinguishing lam. And ma is extra: that is, indeed the matter is that every soul, over it is a guardian. Whoever reads it with the heavy pronunciation, then in (in) is negating, and lamma means "except": that is, not every soul except that over it is a guardian. Ibn ʿAmir, ʿAsim and Hamzah read it here with the heavy pronunciation.

The rest read it with the light pronunciation.

It was said that the guardians (ḥāfiẓ) are the guardian angels who keep record of their deeds, words and actions, and count whatever good and evil they earn. It was said: the guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic. It was said: it is reason, which guides them to what is beneficial and restrains them from what is harmful.

The first view is preferable because of His saying: ﴿And indeed, over you are guardians﴾ [al-Infitar: 10], and His saying: ﴿And He sends over you guardians﴾ [al-Anʿam: 61], and His saying: ﴿For him are successive [angels] before him and behind him, who guard him﴾ [al-Raʿd: 11]. The true Guardian is Allah, Mighty and Majestic, as in His saying: ﴿But Allah is the best guardian﴾ [Yusuf: 64], and the angels' guarding is from His guarding, since they act by His command.

It is said: "I poured the water," meaning I poured it. It is said: "a gushing water" meaning one that is poured, like ﴿a pleasing life﴾ [al-Qariʿah: 7], meaning pleasing.

al-Farra' and al-Akhfash said: "gushing water" means water poured into the womb.

al-Farra' said: The people of the Hijaz often use the active participle with the meaning of the passive in much of their speech, such as "a hidden secret" meaning a concealed one, "hunting" (?) meaning hunted, and "a sleeping night" and similar.

al-Zajjaj said: "from gushing water," that is, water with ejaculation. It is said: dāriʿ, qāyis and nābil, meaning possessor of armour, bow and arrow. Sa'id ibn Jubayr said: they are the neck.

Mujahid said: they are what lies between the shoulders and the chest.

It is also narrated from him that he said: they are the chest, and it is also narrated from him that he said: they are the collarbones.

*If you turn your backs, we shall seize you on your backs; and if you come forward, we shall seize you on your tarā'ib.*

ʿIkrimah said: the tarā'ib are the chest, and he recited:

*A string of pearls upon her tarā'ib*

*And of gold set upon a tarīb, like the colour of ivory, without wrinkles*

*Her tarā'ib are polished like a mirror*

al-Zajjaj related that the tarā'ib are four ribs on the right side of the chest and four ribs on the left side of the chest.

Qatadah and al-Hasan said: the meaning is: it emerges from the loins of the man and the tarā'ib of the woman.
